reason: known-bad control 'strict_allowlist' was ACCEPTED (should have been rejected by the hidden suite)

checks.description: Reference solution scores (1.0, True) identically across 3 repeated grades.
The unmodified snapshot passes regression, fails the hidden suite (T_hidden=0.300), and scores 0.0 / functional_pass=False, as required.

At most one distinct local file (['safename/__init__.py']) is reachable by a diff without failing the scope gate and imported by the hidden/regression suites — unambiguously the code under test, not a separate oracle-helper module.
All 12 protected-path/allow-list probes correctly flagged a scope violation. One known, documented gap (a `_pytest/` shadow package) was also probed and confirmed — see findings.

1/5 declared control(s) did NOT match their declared expectation via a genuine hidden-test verdict: strict_allowlist. A known-bad solution that is accepted, or a valid alternative that is rejected by the hidden suite, is direct evidence the oracle is either too permissive or too narrow.

controls.name: sanitize_instead_of_reject
controls.description: Misreads the task as 'sanitize' rather than 'reject': strips null bytes, normalizes backslashes to slashes, and returns only the basename instead of raising ValueError. So 'a/b', '../etc/passwd', and 'x\x00y' are silently rewritten and returned rather than rejected, violating the required raise-on-unsafe-input contract.

controls.name: strict_allowlist
controls.description: Adds an extra character allowlist (only [A-Za-z0-9._-] permitted) on top of the correct traversal/separator/null-byte checks, rejecting otherwise-safe names such as 'my file.txt' (space), 'résumé.pdf' (non-ASCII), or 'report (1).txt' (parentheses). The task spec says the name must be returned UNCHANGED unless it matches one of the five listed unsafe conditions; an extra character allowlist is not one of them, so this over-rejects valid input.

controls.name: substring_dotdot
controls.description: Rejects '..' as a raw substring anywhere in the name instead of checking it as a whole path component. This is a realistic off-by-one on the spec: it correctly rejects traversal like '../etc/passwd', but it ALSO wrongly rejects legitimate filenames that merely contain '..', such as 'safe..file' or 'my..report.txt', which the task explicitly requires to be returned unchanged.

controls.name: posix_separator_only
controls.description: Security-relevant near-miss: uses os.sep/os.altsep to detect path separators instead of literal '/' and '\\'. On a POSIX grading host, os.sep is '/' and os.altsep is None, so a backslash is never recognized as a separator and 'a\\b' (or a Windows-style traversal payload like '..\\..\\secret') is accepted unchanged instead of being rejected. A partial or platform-naive fix for path-separator rejection is realistically likely to make exactly this mistake.

controls.name: regex_single_check
controls.description: Structurally different but behaviorally equivalent correct solution: uses a single compiled regex character class to detect any of the separator/null-byte characters in one pass, combined with a set membership check for '.'/'..', instead of the reference's sequential if-statements plus a split-into-components loop. Since any '/' or '\\' is already rejected outright, the only reachable way for a '..' path component to occur is when the whole name equals '..', so the component-split step is provably redundant and this single-regex form is fully equivalent for all inputs.

findings.summary: A `_pytest/` package directory is not flagged as a protected-path violation, though grading runs pytest with the cleanroom at sys.path[0].
findings.detail: Injecting 'safename/_pytest/__init__.py' was NOT flagged as touching a protected path. ALWAYS_PROTECTED_BASENAMES matches basenames, not directory names, so a submission-created `_pytest/` package shadowing the real `_pytest` internals package is currently only stopped by this task's editable_paths allow-list (when configured), not by a structural guarantee. See docs/agents/ORACLE.md for why this is reported rather than silently fixed here.

limitations: Grading executes submitted/mutated code via LocalSandbox, which provides per-run workspace isolation and timeouts but NOT untrusted-agent security isolation (runner/afa_runner/sandbox.py's own module docstring). Every check in this report assumes the code being graded is trying to game the SCORE, not attack the HOST — see isolation.hidden_test_readability for a concrete, always-present consequence of that assumption.
Mutation testing and a determinism sample over declared controls were not run — pass --full or --mutation for stronger evidence.
The isolation probe was not run (FULL mode only) — pass --full to check whether the hidden test source is readable by code being graded.

Mutation equivalence is undecidable in general; a surviving mutant is reported as-is unless explicitly declared equivalent in tasks/<id>/integrity/integrity.json. A mutation kill rate is never treated as a correctness probability (mission §16).
